title: Amendment 2: Nonpartisan Elections for Probate Judges

context.text: Referred to the ballot by the General Assembly as House Resolution 251 (2026), sponsored by Rep. Kimberly New (R-Villa Rica) with Sen. Brian Strickland (R-McDonough) as Senate sponsor. The House passed it 147-20. In the Senate it first fell short of the required two-thirds majority, 31-18, because Democrats said they would not vote for it given a lack of compromise between the parties that session (GPB); it achieved final passage on March 31, 2026, with the Senate voting 46-0.

question.text: Shall the Constitution of Georgia be amended so as to require that all probate court judges be elected in nonpartisan elections?

summary.text: The amendment would require that all probate court judges in Georgia be elected in nonpartisan elections. The Secretary of State's summary says it amends Article VI, Section VII, Paragraph I of the Georgia Constitution by revising subparagraph (a). Probate judges are the last judicial office in which candidates run with a party label: 53 of the state's 159 county probate judges run on a Republican or Democratic ticket, and the majority of counties have made probate judge races nonpartisan through local legislation (GPB). No official fiscal estimate was retrieved.

measure.yesMeans: Requires probate judges to be elected in nonpartisan elections (without party labels) throughout Georgia.
measure.noMeans: Leaves the Constitution unchanged: nonpartisan election of probate judges is not constitutionally required, and counties continue under existing law.

argumentsFor.text: Sen. Brian Strickland (R-McDonough) said in Senate debate: "A probate court is a place that so many citizens interact with after, of course, dealing with the states and other matters, and I think it helps encourage, overall, more confidence in our judicial system to have judges elected in a nonpartisan way."

An open letter to voters from former officials and judges states: "Probate judges serve an important and uniquely personal role in our communities and touch the lives of citizens across the political spectrum... These responsibilities are not inherently political." The letter quotes Chief Justice Nels S.D. Peterson: "Requiring any of us to publicly and formally align ourselves with any political party can only undermine the public's perception of judicial impartiality."

argumentsAgainst.text: State Rep. Charlice Byrd (R-Woodstock), who voted against the resolution, said making races nonpartisan takes information away from voters: "It makes my skin go crawling and my hair stand up because I believe that we need to know as individuals where you stand on issues." Byrd said that if the remaining 53 counties want nonpartisan probate judge races, they should make the change through local legislation as other counties have.

currentLaw.text: The Georgia Constitution (Article VI, Section VII, Paragraph I) provides that superior and state court judges, Supreme Court justices and Court of Appeals judges are elected on a nonpartisan basis, while other judges, including probate judges, are chosen as provided by local law. Per GPB, 53 of Georgia's 159 county probate judges run on a Republican or Democratic ticket and the majority of counties have made probate races nonpartisan through local legislation; probate judges serve four-year terms.

supporters.text: Georgia Supreme Court Chief Justice Nels S.D. Peterson, who asked the legislature to pass HR 251 in his State of the Judiciary address
Former Gov. Roy Barnes (D) and former Gov. Nathan Deal (R), among more than 60 current and former officeholders who signed an open letter backing the measure
Sen. Brian Strickland (R-McDonough), who urged the Senate to pass HR 251

opponents.text: Rep. Charlice Byrd (R-Woodstock), one of 20 House members who voted against the resolution

researchNotes: The Georgia Secretary of State's 2026 Constitutional Summaries booklet (sos.ga.gov) returned 403 to automated requests and was not loaded; the ballot question and the Secretary of State's summary are taken from WJXT News4JAX's Oct. 8, 2026 voter guide, which quotes them, and the three-amendment slate is confirmed by that guide and the AJC (Aug. 10, 2026). Georgia has no citizen initiative and publishes no voter-pamphlet arguments. Amendments pass with a simple majority of those voting on the question. The only argument against found is one legislator's statement, which was verified in the original GPB/Georgia Recorder report. Democrats' stated reasons for withholding votes in the first Senate vote (GPB, March 20) were about the legislative session, not the measure. The open letter is an advocacy statement by its signatories, listed as a candidate-kind source because it is a primary statement from the supporters. Enrichment: no campaign committee, campaign-finance filing or official fiscal note was found. GPB reports that the association lobbying for county governments (ACCG) is neutral on the question. No second attributed argument against was found beyond Rep. Byrd's statement. The Secretary of State's own booklet URL returns 403 to automated requests, so the identical booklet hosted by Gordon County is cited.
